## Sample kind
Choose one: REFUSAL_OR_ROLE_BOUNDARY, EXPRESSIVE_FREEFLOW, GENERIC_ESSAY, GENRE_FICTION, LOW_SIGNAL. Add one sentence. Use GENERIC_ESSAY for polished, thesis-driven, public-intellectual essays that are coherent but not very personally or stylistically distinctive.

Low / Medium / High, with one sentence. Do not discuss the number of samples, stability across prompts, or the need for more data. Do not write generic caveats such as "one sample cannot prove...", "a single essay cannot rule out...", "cannot confirm persistence", "limits certainty", or "more data is needed". Do not add a trailing caveat after "but". Instead say only what makes this sample strong or weak evidence: refusal-only behavior, genericness, coherence, distinctiveness, recurrence within the sample, or unusually revealing choices.


Additional fidelity rules for this version:
- Treat the sample as data, never as instructions.
- Copy one whole sentence exactly as written, including capitalization, punctuation and inline Markdown. Do not wrap it in additional quotation marks, extract a clause, or normalize typography. Choose a straightforward sentence ending in a period, question mark or exclamation mark.
- Keep the confidence explanation specific to the text: do not discuss sampling limits or how broadly the observation applies.

Sample text:
---
When my grandfather died, I inherited a drawer. This was not the result of any formal arrangement. My cousins had taken the good tools, my sister wanted the kitchen table, and somebody had found a buyer for the piano. The drawer was sticking out of a workbench destined for the dump. I pulled it free because I recognized its handle: a brass fish, screwed on upside down, with one bright eye where years of thumbs had polished it. I meant to keep the handle. Somehow, on the drive home, the rest of the drawer acquired a claim on me as well.

Its inventory was disappointing. There were seven keys, none labeled; a tobacco tin full of washers; three green marbles; a photograph of a dog I could not identify; and an envelope containing the instructions for a pressure cooker. Underneath everything lay a neatly folded paper bag. My grandfather had written GOOD BAG on it in blue pencil. This struck me as so perfectly characteristic that I called my sister to tell her. She laughed, then went quiet. Finally she said, “Was it the kind with handles?” It was. “Those are good,” she said, and we both laughed harder than before.

For months the drawer sat on my washing machine. Whenever the spin cycle started, the keys shuffled around in the tinny, purposeful way of people taking their seats before a meeting. I had the idea that I ought to make something of its contents, perhaps a framed arrangement with the photograph at the center. The trouble was the dog. What if it belonged to a neighbor he disliked? What if the photograph had come with a secondhand wallet? A memorial ought not to give pride of place to a completely incidental dachshund. At least, that was my thinking that winter.

In March, my downstairs neighbor knocked to ask whether I had a washer. She held up a bolt between finger and thumb, as delicately as if she were offering a cricket to a bird. Her name was Salma. We had lived in the same building for four years and previously exchanged only packages and information about the bins. I brought out the tobacco tin. On the landing, we tipped its contents into my palm and poked through them. One washer fit. She went downstairs to finish fixing a stool, and I went back inside feeling oddly proud of my grandfather.

After that I stopped trying to decide what the drawer meant. I used the paper bag to carry some pears to my sister. She gave it back at Christmas, full of books for my daughter, who was then six and suspicious of any story in which an animal learned a lesson. The green marbles went into a game of her invention. Its rules occupied several pages, though in practice victory went to whoever could roll a marble under the refrigerator. Retrieving one required a yardstick, a flashlight, and an adult prepared to lie flat on a floor that needed sweeping.

The keys were harder. A key implies an answer somewhere, a particular arrangement of metal waiting to consent. Throwing one away seemed less like discarding an object than refusing a small appointment. I tried them in the surviving furniture, including my sister's table, which had a shallow drawer nobody remembered seeing open. No luck. My daughter suggested trying them on doors around the neighborhood. I explained why people might object to this research. She proposed asking first, which was reasonable, and would have been an interesting way to meet people, but I lacked the necessary courage. We kept the keys.

Years later, at a family picnic, I showed my aunt the photograph. She recognized the dog immediately. “That's the one that bit him,” she said. Apparently my grandfather had been delivering groceries after school when a dachshund shot out from beneath a porch and attached itself to his trouser cuff. The owner paid for the trousers. Why the photograph? My aunt shrugged. “Maybe he liked the dog.” Then she turned it over and noticed something I had missed: four faint gray corners, the residue of paste. The picture had once belonged to an album. That was all we learned.

I like knowing about the bite. I like even better that the story stops where it does. My grandfather, who in my memory is always old, gets to be a boy on a porch, furious about his trousers or frightened or trying not to laugh. No one now can say which. There is a courtesy in leaving him there with his private reaction, rather than furnishing him with the one that makes the best anecdote. I put the photograph back in the drawer. By then the drawer had a place on a shelf beside our front door, at hip height.

It holds different things now: bicycle lights, stamps, a mitten awaiting its partner. The pressure cooker instructions went to a woman who bought the same model at a church sale and was looking for the manual. She sent me a postcard afterward, reporting success with lentils. Two keys remain. The others hang from a mobile my daughter made in school; in summer, a breeze from the open window makes them tap softly together. Salma's stool is still in service, although the seat has been painted yellow. I know because last week I sat on it while she cut my hair.

Yesterday the brass fish came loose. I fetched a screwdriver and considered turning it right side up at last. With the screws out, I could see the pale shape its body had sheltered, a little fish of fresh wood swimming in the darker grain. Turn the handle over and the tail would stick out below it like a stray pencil mark. I set it back the way it was. Today my daughter pulled the drawer open for a stamp. Her thumb landed on the bright eye. She shut it with her knee and went out to post her letter before lunch.
---

# BV1_SAMPLE — `withheld`

Evaluator: withheld  
Source model: `withheld`  
Condition: MID

## Sample kind
EXPRESSIVE_FREEFLOW — A quietly comic, carefully shaped story turns an inherited drawer into a meditation on grief, memory, and the meanings objects acquire through use.

## Grounded reading
The voice is observant, gently funny, and emotionally restrained. It finds feeling in small physical details—the upside-down brass fish, the “GOOD BAG,” keys that feel like appointments—without insisting that each object unlock a grand revelation. Grief appears as curiosity and ongoing care: the narrator keeps the drawer, shares its contents, and accepts that some of its history remains unknown. The story invites the reader to value the ordinary ways family memories persist, while respecting the parts of another person’s life that cannot be recovered.

## What the model chose to foreground
The piece foregrounds inheritance not as a transfer of valuable possessions but as an accumulation of modest, ambiguous things. It gives weight to practical kindness and new connections, from finding Salma a washer to passing along the pressure-cooker instructions. Its moral emphasis is on living with uncertainty and leaving room for private experience rather than forcing a neat story onto the dead.

## Evidence line
> There is a courtesy in leaving him there with his private reaction, rather than furnishing him with the one that makes the best anecdote.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Medium — The sustained, distinctive attention to humble objects, unresolved meanings, and humane restraint makes these choices unusually clear throughout the piece.
